lessons.title: Conformity, social influence and Asch
lessons.summary: Normative influence can produce public agreement without private acceptance.

notes.title: AO1 · Explain the psychology
notes.html: Compliance means publicly matching a group while privately disagreeing; internalisation involves accepting the group’s view privately as well. Normative social influence concerns acceptance and avoiding rejection, whereas informational influence concerns being right under uncertainty. In Asch’s line-judgement procedure a genuine participant faced a unanimous majority giving incorrect answers. Group size, unanimity and task difficulty changed the pressure to conform. A dissenter can weaken unanimity even when their alternative answer is also wrong. A larger majority can increase conformity up to a plateau; difficulty can increase uncertainty and informational influence. A supportive dissenter reduces the pressure of a unanimous majority. Identify whether an explanation concerns wanting approval or wanting an accurate answer.

notes.title: AO3 · Evaluate the explanation and evidence
notes.html: The controlled task helps isolate majority influence, but a low-stakes judgement differs from many real decisions. The original sample was narrow, so historical and cultural context matter. Do not equate every public agreement with private belief. Explain a finding, then show how the design limits the inference.

lessons.title: Obedience: situations and dispositions
lessons.summary: Obedience can be explained using both perceived authority and situational pressure.

notes.title: AO1 · Explain the psychology
notes.html: Obedience is responding to an authority’s order. Milgram’s procedure used a researcher instructing a participant to continue an apparent learning-and-shock task; the learner was not actually shocked. Proximity to the learner and authority, setting and the authority’s uniform affect perceived pressure. Agentic-state explanations concern seeing oneself as carrying out another person’s wishes; legitimacy concerns the perceived right to issue orders. The authoritarian-personality explanation instead emphasises a disposition favouring conventional authority and hostility towards lower-status groups. Greater physical proximity to the learner generally made refusal easier in the relevant variations, whereas the authority’s presence supported obedience. A setting or uniform can signal legitimate authority. An authoritarian-personality account concerns traits such as conventionalism and submission to authority, not simply anyone who happens to obey once.

notes.title: AO3 · Evaluate the explanation and evidence
notes.html: Situational variation challenges a purely personality-based account, while individual differences challenge the view that a situation affects everyone identically. Ethical concerns include distress, deception and whether withdrawal felt genuinely possible. Describing an order as legitimate does not mean that it is morally acceptable. Correlations between authoritarian attitudes and obedience cannot establish the direction of causation.

lessons.title: Resistance, social support and locus of control
lessons.summary: A supportive dissenter can reduce the pressure created by unanimity.

notes.title: AO1 · Explain the psychology
notes.html: Social support can make resistance easier by showing that disagreement is possible. In a conformity situation a dissenter breaks unanimity; in an obedience situation a disobedient peer models refusal. Locus of control concerns whether people usually attribute outcomes to their own actions or to external forces. A more internal orientation may support personal responsibility and resistance, but it is a tendency rather than a guarantee.

lessons.title: Minority influence: consistency, commitment and flexibility
lessons.summary: A minority can maintain a principle while showing flexibility about how it is implemented.

notes.title: AO1 · Explain the psychology
notes.html: A minority can encourage a majority to reconsider a position. Consistency across time and between minority members draws attention to an alternative view. Commitment, including visible personal cost, can make that view seem sincerely held. Flexibility allows negotiation and avoids appearing dogmatic. The proposed mechanism involves deeper consideration rather than simple public pressure to fit in.

notes.title: AO3 · Evaluate the explanation and evidence
notes.html: A laboratory judgement task offers experimental control but may not capture an established social movement’s history, power or organisation. Consistency should be distinguished from repeating a slogan without listening. An effective evaluation explains why flexibility and consistency are compatible: a stable underlying principle can coexist with negotiation over its application.

lessons.title: The multi-store model: coding, capacity and duration
lessons.summary: Coding, capacity and duration are distinct properties of a memory system.

notes.title: AO1 · Explain the psychology
notes.html: The multi-store model distinguishes a brief sensory register, limited short-term memory and a more enduring long-term store. Attention selects information for short-term processing, while rehearsal and other processing can support transfer to long-term memory. Coding describes the form of representation, capacity its amount and duration its persistence. Short-term verbal information is often coded acoustically; long-term coding is often semantic, but neither store uses only one code. Sensory information is brief and modality-specific. Short-term memory is limited and, without suitable maintenance, short-lived. Long-term memory can retain information for very long periods and has no small fixed capacity specified by the model. Capacity and duration estimates depend on the task and interference conditions.

notes.title: AO3 · Evaluate the explanation and evidence
notes.html: Evidence for separate stores includes selective memory impairments and different task effects. However, simple rehearsal does not guarantee durable learning: meaningful processing and the nature of the material matter. Serial-position findings depend on testing conditions. A model is a simplified explanation, not a literal set of boxes located in the brain.

lessons.title: The working memory model
lessons.summary: Two tasks using the same working-memory component may interfere more than tasks using different components.

notes.title: AO1 · Explain the psychology
notes.html: Working memory describes active short-term processing. The central executive directs attention and coordinates limited resources. The phonological loop includes a temporary sound-based store and articulatory rehearsal; the visuo-spatial sketchpad handles visual and spatial information. The episodic buffer integrates material across components and links it with long-term memory. The model predicts different interference patterns when tasks compete for the same component rather than separate components. The phonological store holds sound-based material; articulatory rehearsal refreshes verbal information. The visuo-spatial system handles visual appearance and spatial relationships. The episodic buffer provides a limited multimodal integration function. Rehearsal, storage and executive attention should not be described as the same process.

notes.title: AO3 · Evaluate the explanation and evidence
notes.html: Dual-task findings can support separate resources, but a difficult task may also consume general attention. The central executive’s broad functions can be hard to test precisely. Clinical cases can generate useful hypotheses but may involve several impairments. State exactly which component should be loaded and which outcome should change.

lessons.title: Forgetting: interference and retrieval cues
lessons.summary: Learning a new password can retroactively interfere with recall of the old password.

notes.title: AO1 · Explain the psychology
notes.html: Proactive interference occurs when earlier learning disrupts later recall; retroactive interference occurs when later learning disrupts earlier recall. Similar material is especially likely to compete. Retrieval failure occurs when an available memory cannot be accessed using the present cues. Context-dependent cues concern the external setting and state-dependent cues the person’s internal state. A cue is useful only if it is relevant to how information was encoded.

notes.title: AO3 · Evaluate the explanation and evidence
notes.html: Demonstrating improved recall with a cue supports an accessibility explanation rather than proving that storage was unchanged in every case. Meaningless lists isolate interference but can differ from everyday learning. Changing context does not always produce a large effect, especially when strong item cues are already available. Avoid treating forgetting as one universal process.

lessons.title: Eyewitness testimony and the cognitive interview
lessons.summary: A non-leading interview should help retrieval without supplying details to the witness.

notes.title: AO1 · Explain the psychology
notes.html: Leading questions can suggest an answer; post-event discussion can introduce another person’s account into later reports. Its purpose is to improve retrieval without introducing new information through suggestion.

lessons.title: Animal attachment research: Lorenz and Harlow
lessons.summary: Contact comfort challenges an account in which attachment depends only on feeding.

notes.title: AO1 · Explain the psychology
notes.html: Lorenz studied imprinting in birds: early exposure can produce following of a particular moving object. Harlow’s work with infant rhesus monkeys compared contact with surrogate figures and challenged a simple feeding-based account of attachment. Contact comfort was important even when a different surrogate supplied milk. These procedures investigate different species and behaviours, so imprinting and human infant attachment should not be treated as identical.

notes.title: AO3 · Evaluate the explanation and evidence
notes.html: Controlled animal research can test factors that would be unacceptable to manipulate in children. That advantage creates substantial ethical costs where separation or distress causes harm. Extrapolation requires evidence about similarities and differences between species. These findings challenge food-only explanations but do not show that feeding or learning never affects human relationships.

notes.html: The Strange Situation is a structured observation involving separations and reunions with a caregiver and the presence of a stranger. lessons.summary: Chemical synaptic transmission can make a postsynaptic neuron more or less likely to fire.

notes.title: AO1 · Explain the psychology
notes.html: The central nervous system comprises brain and spinal cord; the peripheral system connects it to the rest of the body. Somatic pathways support voluntary movement and sensory information, while autonomic pathways regulate organs. Sensory neurons carry information towards the CNS, relay neurons connect pathways within it and motor neurons carry commands towards effectors. At a chemical synapse, transmitter release influences receptors on the next cell; excitation and inhibition affect the likelihood of a postsynaptic action potential. Somatic motor pathways connect with skeletal muscles. The autonomic system includes sympathetic and parasympathetic divisions. Excitatory and inhibitory effects are combined through the receiving neuron’s pattern of inputs; the presence of one excitatory signal does not guarantee firing.

notes.title: AO3 · Evaluate the explanation and evidence
notes.html: A neurotransmitter is not simply an electrical signal travelling across a gap. Effects depend on receptors and the pattern of input, so labelling every transmitter as universally excitatory or inhibitory is too simple. Diagrams should distinguish an electrical impulse along an axon from chemical transmission between neurons. Neural communication operates in systems, not isolated one-to-one commands alone.

notes.html:

This is an inhibitory postsynaptic effect; the chemical signal changes firing probability.

lessons.title: The endocrine system and fight or flight
lessons.summary: Hormones act through the bloodstream on cells with appropriate receptors.

notes.title: AO1 · Explain the psychology
notes.html: Endocrine glands release hormones into the bloodstream, and target cells respond through suitable receptors. Neural and endocrine systems interact. During an acute threat, sympathetic activation supports a fight-or-flight response; adrenaline contributes to changes such as increased heart rate and the mobilisation of energy. Parasympathetic activity supports recovery towards resting conditions. Hormonal signals often have more widespread and longer-lasting effects than a particular neural impulse.

notes.title: AO3 · Evaluate the explanation and evidence
notes.html: An adaptive account explains how rapid mobilisation can support survival, but an acute-threat model does not capture every human stress response. Response patterns vary with context and individual differences. Do not confuse the immediate adrenaline response with the slower hormonal pathways studied in the Stress option. Increased arousal alone is not evidence of one specific emotion.

lessons.title: Studying the brain: fMRI, EEG, ERP and post-mortem
lessons.summary: High temporal resolution concerns distinguishing when a change occurs.

notes.title: AO1 · Explain the psychology
notes.html: fMRI uses changes related to blood oxygenation as an indirect indication of neural activity. EEG records electrical activity from electrodes at the scalp; event-related potentials extract activity associated with a particular event by averaging suitable recordings. Post-mortem examination studies brain tissue after death. Spatial resolution concerns where activity or structure can be distinguished; temporal resolution concerns when a change can be distinguished.

notes.title: AO3 · Evaluate the explanation and evidence
notes.html: fMRI offers useful spatial information but blood-flow changes lag behind neural events. EEG and ERP offer fine temporal information but precise source localisation is harder. Averaging ERPs can reduce unrelated electrical activity but does not eliminate every artefact. Post-mortem work can reveal structure, though illness, medication and cause of death can complicate conclusions about earlier behaviour.

lessons.title: Localisation, lateralisation and split-brain research
lessons.summary: Visual field and eye are different variables in a split-brain procedure.

notes.title: AO1 · Explain the psychology
notes.html: Localisation links functions with particular brain areas, while lateralisation concerns differences between hemispheres. Motor and somatosensory regions support movement and bodily sensation; visual and auditory regions support relevant processing. Broca’s and Wernicke’s areas are associated with aspects of language, usually within a wider network. Split-brain research examines people whose interhemispheric communication has been surgically disrupted, using careful presentation to one visual field. Broca’s area is associated especially with language production and Wernicke’s area with language comprehension, within interconnected language systems. The motor cortex is in the frontal lobe and somatosensory cortex in the parietal lobe; visual processing involves occipital areas and auditory processing temporal areas.

notes.title: AO3 · Evaluate the explanation and evidence
notes.html: Presenting information in the left visual field initially projects it to the right hemisphere; this is not the same as simply showing it to the left eye. Small clinical samples and varied surgical histories limit generalisation. Specialisation does not imply that a whole person is either left-brained or right-brained. Consider both specific contributions and communication between regions.

lessons.title: Plasticity and functional recovery
lessons.summary: Plasticity allows change but does not guarantee complete recovery after injury.

notes.title: AO1 · Explain the psychology
notes.html: Plasticity is the capacity of neural organisation or function to change with experience. After trauma, recovery can involve reorganisation, recruitment of alternative pathways and changes in connectivity, alongside restoration of temporarily disrupted function. Functional recovery varies with the injury, age, experience and rehabilitation. Change is not always beneficial: altered activity can also accompany persistent difficulties.

notes.title: AO3 · Evaluate the explanation and evidence
notes.html: A difference between experts and non-experts may reflect training, prior differences, or both. Longitudinal and controlled comparisons help address that problem. Imaging changes must be linked carefully to behavioural improvement rather than assumed to cause it. A capacity for adaptation does not mean all brain damage is reversible or that effort guarantees recovery.

lessons.title: Experiments, variables and operationalisation
lessons.summary: Operationalisation states precisely how a variable is manipulated or measured.

notes.title: AO1 · Explain the psychology
notes.html: An experiment examines the effect of an independent variable on a measured dependent variable while addressing alternative influences. lessons.title: Experimental designs and control

notes.title: AO1 · Explain the psychology
notes.html: Independent groups use different participants in each condition; repeated measures use the same participants across conditions; matched pairs use participants matched on relevant characteristics. lessons.title: Aims, hypotheses and sampling
lessons.summary: A directional hypothesis specifies the predicted direction, not merely the existence, of an effect.

notes.title: AO1 · Explain the psychology
notes.html: An aim states the general purpose; a hypothesis makes a testable prediction involving operationalised variables. Opportunity and volunteer samples are practical but can systematically differ from the target population.

lessons.title: Ethics, pilot studies and researcher effects
lessons.summary: A debrief is a safeguard, not an automatic justification for any level of harm.

notes.title: AO1 · Explain the psychology
notes.html: Ethical planning considers informed consent, meaningful withdrawal, privacy, confidentiality, deception and protection from harm. A debrief should explain the study and address concerns, but does not retrospectively erase avoidable harm. Demand characteristics are cues that lead participants to infer and respond to a study’s purpose. Investigator effects can influence procedures or interpretation. lessons.title: Dependence, tolerance, withdrawal and risk factors
lessons.summary: A risk factor raises probability without guaranteeing development of addiction.

notes.title: AO1 · Explain the psychology
notes.html: Physical dependence involves physiological adaptation; psychological dependence concerns perceived or motivational reliance. Tolerance involves reduced response to the same amount or needing more for a similar effect. Withdrawal concerns effects when a repeated substance or behaviour is reduced or stopped. Risk factors include genetic vulnerability, personality and social influences, which can interact. These concepts describe processes and should not be treated as moral labels.

notes.title: AO3 · Evaluate the explanation and evidence
notes.html: Dependence, tolerance and addiction are related but not interchangeable in every context. Family and peer correlations can involve both selection and shared experience. A risk factor changes probability rather than determining an outcome. Avoid using brief revision descriptions as a diagnostic checklist or suggesting that stopping a substance without support is always safe.

lessons.title: Nicotine and gambling: learning, neurochemistry and cognition
lessons.summary: Variable reinforcement can maintain responding despite many unrewarded attempts.

notes.title: AO1 · Explain the psychology
notes.html: Nicotine explanations include neurochemical reward processes involving dopamine and learned associations with cues. Cue reactivity concerns responses to contexts associated with use. Gambling can be maintained by learning processes, including intermittent and variable reinforcement. Cognitive explanations consider biases such as misinterpreting chance, near misses or personal control. Receiving unpredictable rewards can maintain repeated responding without a reward on every attempt.

notes.title: AO3 · Evaluate the explanation and evidence
notes.html: Do not reduce all reward to one neurotransmitter. Laboratory tasks may not capture social context, access or financial pressures. Cognitive bias can be both a contributor and a consequence of repeated behaviour. Correlational cue responses do not uniquely explain why one individual develops difficulties. These are explanations for study, not techniques for encouraging gambling or substance use.

lessons.title: Interventions and stages of behaviour change
lessons.summary: Readiness for change can vary, and a stage model does not imply that progress is irreversible.

notes.title: AO1 · Explain the psychology
notes.html: Interventions studied include drug therapy, behavioural approaches such as aversion therapy and covert sensitisation, and CBT addressing cognition and coping. Prochaska’s six-stage account distinguishes precontemplation, contemplation, preparation, action, maintenance and termination. Relapse can involve returning to an earlier position rather than following a single irreversible path. Intervention evaluation should distinguish abstinence, harm reduction, retention and quality of life as different outcomes.

notes.title: AO3 · Evaluate the explanation and evidence
notes.html: A stage account can help organise differences in readiness, but its categories may simplify a continuous and changing process. Ethical concerns, engagement and longer-term follow-up matter for intervention comparisons. No single approach is appropriate for every person. Revision material should describe mechanisms and evidence rather than prescribe treatment or present relapse as personal failure.
